Extensive branching produces many narrow capillaries and a large total exchange area. Their narrow lumens bring blood cells close to the wall. A single endothelial-cell layer makes the exchange distance short.

Dissolved substances move between blood and the surrounding environment according to their gradients and the wall’s permeability. interactions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from capillary branching and exchange?

options.text: Thin endothelial walls and branching capillary beds support exchange.
options.feedback: Correct: Dissolved oxygen and nutrients cross capillary walls into tissue fluid, while wastes can move toward blood along gradients. options.text: All capillaries have thick muscular walls.

options.text: Every capillary has large fenestrations.
options.feedback: Only some capillary beds are fenestrated; most exchange occurs across very thin endothelial walls.

options.text: Capillaries are wide tubes that keep erythrocytes far from exchange surfaces.
options.feedback: Their narrow lumens shorten the effective diffusion distance between blood and tissues.

recall.explanation: Capillaries are numerous microscopic blood vessels forming extensive branching beds, creating a large total area for exchange with tissues. Their narrow lumens place erythrocytes near the endothelium and slow passage through the network; most walls are a single endothelial-cell layer with a thin underlying basal lamina.

sections.guidingQuestion: Recognize arteries and veins in cross section?
sections.explanation:
Arteries generally have a thicker muscular and elastic wall relative to their lumen. Veins generally have thinner walls and a wider, sometimes flattened lumen; some show valves. Both have an endothelial lining and supporting tissues.

Use wall-to-lumen ratio and tissue layers when identifying a micrograph, since preparation can distort shape. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it. Oxygen content does not define them: pulmonary arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

options.text: Elastic arterial walls damp pulsatility and preserve downstream flow.
options.feedback: Correct: During systole arterial expansion temporarily stores energy; during diastole elastic recoil maintains forward flow while ventricular ejection pauses. options.feedback: Collagen resists overextension, elasticity stores and releases energy, and muscle alters diameter.

sections.guidingQuestion: Measure the pulse without confusing it with flow?
sections.explanation:
Feel the radial or carotid pulse gently with fingertips, count beats over a measured interval and convert to beats per minute. For example, 18 beats in 15 seconds gives 18 × 4 = 72 beats min⁻¹. A longer interval or repeated counts reduces the effect of a single missed beat.

A pulse is an arterial pressure wave associated with ventricular ejection, not the velocity of an individual red blood cell. Compare manual counts with a digital sensor under similar conditions; movement, missed beats and measurement timing can affect agreement.

sections.explanation:
Veins return blood at lower pressure than arteries. Their relatively thin, flexible walls can be compressed by contracting skeletal muscles, helping propel blood toward the heart.

Valves in many peripheral veins close against reverse flow when pressure changes, directing muscle-assisted movement toward the heart. They do not generate pressure themselves. Breathing-associated pressure changes also assist venous return; not every vein contains valves.

sections.guidingQuestion: Cohesion and evaporation pull xylem water?
sections.explanation:
Water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out through stomata. Replacement water is drawn from xylem through connected cell-wall spaces by capillary action, generating tension: negative pressure potential in the xylem.

Cohesion through hydrogen bonding maintains a continuous water column, transmitting tension downward and drawing water upward from roots. Adhesion helps maintain contact with vessel walls, while evaporation-generated tension is the main driver of water ascent in actively transpiring plants, rather than an ATP-driven root water pump. When stomata close, water-vapour loss generally slows, reducing the transpiration pull.
sections.revisionSummary: Evaporation draws water through cell walls from xylem by capillary action, creating tension. Cohesion maintains a continuous column that transmits the pull downward and draws water upward.

sections.guidingQuestion: Xylem vessel elements are built for tension?
sections.explanation:
Mature xylem vessel elements are dead and lack cell contents. Incomplete or absent end walls connect them into long conduits with low resistance to bulk water flow.

Lignified walls withstand the tensions generated during transpiration and help prevent inward collapse. Pits permit water to enter or leave sideways between vessels and nearby tissues. Hollow tubes, reinforced walls and pits solve different transport problems; the cells do not actively pump water.

sections.guidingQuestion: Tissue fluid exchanges with living cells?
sections.explanation:
Plasma is the fluid component of blood, containing water, ions, nutrients, wastes, hormones and proteins. Tissue fluid forms mainly from plasma filtration, has fewer large plasma proteins and normally lacks red blood cells. It surrounds and bathes tissue cells.

Oxygen and nutrients cross from capillary blood through tissue fluid and then the cell membrane. Carbon dioxide and other wastes can move the other way, according to gradients and membrane transport mechanisms. Circulation renews the supply and removes products; blood does not normally flow directly over the cells.

sections.guidingQuestion: Single fish versus double mammalian circulation?
sections.explanation:
In bony fish, blood follows heart → gill capillaries → body tissues → heart. It gains oxygen at the gills and loses pressure across the gill capillaries before reaching systemic tissues. It passes through the heart once per complete circuit.

Returning to the heart between pulmonary and systemic capillary beds allows re-pressurization for the body while maintaining lower pulmonary pressure. sections.guidingQuestion: Cardiac cycle: filling, pressure and ejection?
sections.explanation:
Sinoatrial excitation leads to atrial contraction and completion of ventricular filling. Left ventricular contraction raises pressure, closing the atrioventricular valve. When ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic semilunar valve opens and blood is ejected.

As the left ventricle relaxes, arterial pressure closes the aortic valve. The atrioventricular valve opens when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, allowing filling. Systolic arterial pressure is the higher value during ejection; diastolic is the lower value between beats. In an illustrative 120/80 mmHg reading, these are 120 and 80 mmHg respectively; valves respond to pressure, rather than opening by active muscular action.

sections.guidingQuestion: Root pressure operates when transpiration is weak?
sections.explanation:
Root tissues actively transport mineral ions into the xylem using energy ultimately supplied by respiration. This creates a higher solute concentration in the xylem than in the surrounding root tissues and therefore lowers the water potential of xylem fluid. Water is not moved directly along a xylem vessel by an ATP-driven water pump; ATP-dependent ion transport establishes the water-potential difference.

Water moves into xylem from neighbouring root tissues down the water-potential gradient. In conditions that restrict evaporation from leaves, continued osmotic water entry can raise pressure potential inside the vessels above atmospheric pressure. This positive pressure is called root pressure. It can push water up stems for limited distances and can contribute to guttation, in which liquid droplets appear at leaf margins.

Root pressure becomes relatively noticeable when transpiration is low—for example during humid weather or in spring before deciduous trees have developed leaves. By contrast, evaporation from leaves generates tension (negative pressure) in xylem; cohesion–tension is the dominant explanation for water ascent in tall, actively transpiring plants. A high humidity observation is therefore not proof that root pressure is the principal driving force at midday in every species.
sections.revisionSummary: Active mineral loading lowers xylem water potential; osmotic entry raises positive pressure. It is more important when transpiration is insufficient, such as high humidity or before spring leaf opening.
sections.workedExample: Predict the effect of a humid night: transpiration becomes weak, but active mineral loading may continue, so osmotic entry can produce measurable positive xylem pressure in suitable plants.

sections.explanation:
Living sieve-tube elements have no nucleus, reduced cytoplasm and fewer organelles, leaving space for sap. Sieve plates connect successive elements and allow flow through the tube.

Companion cells retain nuclei, abundant mitochondria and plasmodesmata connecting them to sieve-tube elements. Their metabolism supports loading carbon compounds at sources and unloading at sinks. Loading can draw in water and raise source pressure, driving bulk flow toward lower-pressure sinks. Phloem direction is source-to-sink, not universally upward or downward.

terms: Sieve tube element: living phloem conducting cell with a sieve plate and no mature nucleus
Companion cell: metabolically active cell linked to a sieve tube element
Source: region exporting sugars, often a mature photosynthesizing leaf
Sink: region importing sugars for use or storage, such as a growing fruit

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from capillary branching and exchange?

options.text: Thin endothelial walls and branching capillary beds support exchange.
options.feedback: Correct: Dissolved oxygen and nutrients cross capillary walls into tissue fluid, while wastes can move toward blood along gradients. Some capillaries have fenestrations that increase permeability, for example at sites needing rapid fluid exchange. Fenestrations are not universally present, and capillaries do not all permit proteins to pass freely.

options.text: All capillaries have thick muscular walls.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Fenestrations occur only in particular capillary beds, so an answer claiming every capillary has large pores would be anatomically wrong. The proposed answer, “All capillaries have thick muscular walls.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Every capillary has large fenestrations.
options.feedback: Only some capillary beds are fenestrated; most exchange occurs across very thin endothelial walls.

options.text: Capillaries are wide tubes that keep erythrocytes far from exchange surfaces.
options.feedback: Their narrow lumens shorten the effective diffusion distance between blood and tissues.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from recognize arteries and veins in cross section?

options.text: An artery carries blood away from the heart, with a thick resilient wall adapted to its pressure.
options.feedback: Correct: Both vessel classes have endothelial linings and outer connective tissue. Identify them by wall-to-lumen ratio and wall layers rather than by blood oxygen concentration, because pulmonary arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins oxygenated blood. Section shape can be affected by tissue preparation.

options.text: Arteries always contain oxygen-rich blood.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Vessel identity depends on direction relative to the heart; pressure, wall thickness and lumen shape are stronger histological clues than colour coding. The proposed answer, “Arteries always contain oxygen-rich blood.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Veins usually have thicker muscular walls than similar-sized arteries.
options.feedback: At comparable size, arteries characteristically have a thicker tunica media relative to their lumen.

options.text: Pulmonary blood oxygenation alone distinguishes an artery from a vein.
options.feedback: Pulmonary veins are oxygenated despite carrying blood toward the heart.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from arterial walls withstand pulsatile pressure?

options.text: Elastic arterial walls damp pulsatility and preserve downstream flow.
options.feedback: Correct: During systole arterial expansion temporarily stores energy; during diastole elastic recoil maintains forward flow while ventricular ejection pauses. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, not necessarily toward an oxygenated tissue. Excessive rigidity can interfere with this pressure-buffering function.

options.text: Arterial pressure drops to zero between heartbeats.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Elastic fibres restore stored wall energy during diastole, while smooth muscle adjusts resistance; these tissues are not interchangeable. The proposed answer, “Arterial pressure drops to zero between heartbeats.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Elastic recoil stops completely once ventricular ejection ends.
options.feedback: Elastic recoil sustains downstream flow during diastole.

options.text: Collagen and smooth muscle have exactly the same function as elastic tissue.
options.feedback: Collagen resists overextension, elasticity stores and releases energy, and muscle alters diameter.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from measure the pulse without confusing it with flow?

options.text: A pulse is an arterial pressure wave normally associated with each ventricular beat.
options.feedback: Correct: Count beats for a timed interval and convert to beats per minute, preferably after rest and with repeated trials. Compare manual counting with a validated optical sensor and note motion artefacts. Pulse rate estimates heart rate during a regular rhythm, but it is not the speed at which individual red cells travel.

options.text: A pulse records blood velocity directly.
options.feedback: Incorrect: A 15-second count is multiplied by four to obtain beats min⁻¹; count errors are also multiplied by four, which favours longer or repeated measurements. The proposed answer, “A pulse records blood velocity directly.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: The pulse count records how fast one erythrocyte travels.
options.feedback: A palpable pulse is a pressure wave, not individual red-cell velocity.

options.text: An 18-beat count in 15 seconds equals 18 beats per minute.
options.feedback: The correct conversion multiplies by four, giving 72 beats per minute.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from venous valves and skeletal-muscle pumping?

options.text: Muscle compression and one-way valves assist venous return.
options.feedback: Correct: Contraction of nearby muscles squeezes venous segments and propels blood toward the heart, with the direction constrained by valves. Respiratory pressure changes and the heart's pumping also contribute to venous return. Not all veins contain valves, so it is inaccurate to call valves universal.

options.text: Vein valves generate pressure through active contraction.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Valves restrict reflux only in veins where they are present; they do not generate the pressure required to move blood. The proposed answer, “Vein valves generate pressure through active contraction.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Venous valves generate the pressure that returns blood to the heart.
options.feedback: Valves prevent reversal; muscle compression and pressure differences drive return.

options.text: Every vein contains valves, including all central veins.
options.feedback: Valves occur in many peripheral veins, not universally.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from coronary blockage and evidence?

options.text: Coronary disease interpretation requires mechanistic evidence and carefully controlled population data.
options.feedback: Correct: Epidemiological correlations between risk factors and coronary heart disease require careful interpretation. Smoking, blood pressure, plasma lipids, diabetes, socioeconomic conditions and age can be confounders. A high correlation coefficient describes association, not proof of a specific causal pathway; compare populations, methods and absolute rates.

options.text: Every high correlation proves causation.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Relative risk, incidence, a correlation coefficient and a causal effect are distinct quantities; any illustrative risk table must be identified as synthetic. The proposed answer, “Every high correlation proves causation.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: An epidemiological correlation establishes that a risk factor caused disease.
options.feedback: Even a strong association requires control for confounding and mechanistic evidence before causal inference.

options.text: A thrombus in a coronary artery cannot affect the myocardium.
options.feedback: Coronary occlusion deprives myocardium of oxygen and may trigger infarction.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from cohesion and evaporation pull xylem water?

options.text: Evaporation in leaves generates tension that pulls a continuous cohesive xylem column.
options.feedback: Correct: Hydrogen bonding supplies cohesion between water molecules, preventing the stretched column from fragmenting under ordinary conditions. Adhesion and capillary interactions help wet narrow walls and transfer water through cell-wall spaces, but evaporation-generated tension is the main driver of high-tree transport. No transpiration-powered pump is located at the roots.

options.text: Xylem water is pushed up solely by roots.
options.feedback: Incorrect: The transpiration stream is largely a passive physical process within dead xylem vessels; energy expenditure elsewhere in the plant does not constitute a xylem pump. The proposed answer, “Xylem water is pushed up solely by roots.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: A tall tree lifts xylem water using ATP-driven vessel pumps.
options.feedback: The main ascent mechanism is evaporation-generated tension transmitted by cohesive water.

options.text: Water climbs because xylem sap is always at positive pressure.
options.feedback: During active transpiration xylem commonly experiences negative pressure potential.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from xylem vessel elements are built for tension?

options.text: Hollow lignified vessels permit low-resistance water flow under negative pressure.
options.feedback: Correct: Lignified secondary walls reinforce the conduit against collapse under negative pressure, often forming rings, helices or pits according to cell type. Pits in side walls allow lateral movement into adjacent conduits and surrounding cells. An embolism can block a vessel; redundant networks help maintain transport.

options.text: Xylem vessels need living nuclei to pump water.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Lignin reinforces the conduit against inward collapse during tension, while pits permit lateral movement; these adaptations serve different mechanical roles. The proposed answer, “Xylem vessels need living nuclei to pump water.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Mature xylem vessel elements need a nucleus to pump water.
options.feedback: Mature conducting elements are hollow and lack living contents; movement is largely passive.

options.text: Pits are the thickest impermeable parts of xylem walls.
options.feedback: Pits enable lateral water movement between conduits and neighbouring tissues.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from map vascular bundles in dicot stems?

options.text: Dicot stem bundles commonly form a peripheral ring with xylem inward and phloem outward.
options.feedback: Correct: A low-power transverse plan should show the relative positions of epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles, pith and xylem versus phloem. Label tissue regions rather than inventing cell-level features not visible at that magnification. Use authentic stem micrographs to verify the pattern; atypical species may differ.

options.text: Dicot stem vascular bundles are always scattered randomly.
options.feedback: Incorrect: A low-power plan should locate the vascular bundle ring, with phloem toward the cortex and xylem toward the pith, rather than drawing invented cells. The proposed answer, “Dicot stem vascular bundles are always scattered randomly.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: In a young dicot stem, xylem is exterior to phloem.
options.feedback: Typical vascular bundles have xylem inward and phloem outward.

options.text: Young dicot stems place all vascular tissue in a central star.
options.feedback: The bundles commonly form a peripheral ring around the pith.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from recognize transport tissue in dicot roots?

options.text: Dicot root xylem is central, with phloem between xylem arms.
options.feedback: Correct: Draw a clean low-power plan from an authenticated root section, distinguishing epidermis, cortex and the central stele. Indicate xylem and phloem accurately and do not confuse the endodermis with the outer epidermis. Species and root age influence vascular anatomy; a teaching schematic expresses the typical case.

options.text: Root xylem always forms an outer ring beneath the cuticle.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Root and stem arrangements should not be swapped: the central star-like xylem is characteristic of many young dicot roots, not young dicot stems. The proposed answer, “Root xylem always forms an outer ring beneath the cuticle.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: The outermost tissue in a root is the endodermis.
options.feedback: The epidermis is outermost, while the endodermis encloses the vascular cylinder.

options.text: Typical dicot roots have a peripheral ring of xylem bundles exactly like a stem.
options.feedback: A young dicot root often shows central star-shaped xylem with phloem between the arms.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from tissue-fluid pressure filtration and return?

options.text: Fluid movement depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces, with lymphatic return important.
options.feedback: Correct: The syllabus describes lower venular pressure allowing some fluid re-entry. Modern revised Starling physiology emphasizes that sustained venular reabsorption is often limited in most systemic capillaries and lymphatics return much filtered volume. Present schematic pressure gradients as a simplified syllabus model while noting context, endothelial glycocalyx and tissue-specific exceptions.

options.text: Every filtered molecule must return through the venous end of the same capillary.
options.feedback: Incorrect: The simplified syllabus describes possible venular re-entry, but sustained reabsorption is often limited in most systemic beds under the revised Starling model. The proposed answer, “Every filtered molecule must return through the venous end of the same capillary.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: All systemic capillary filtrate is permanently reabsorbed at the venous end.
options.feedback: Sustained reabsorption is not universal; lymphatics return much of the filtered volume.

options.text: Tissue fluid consists mainly of escaped intact red blood cells.
options.feedback: Tissue fluid is predominantly filtered plasma, with blood cells and most large proteins retained.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from tissue fluid exchanges with living cells?

options.text: Interstitial fluid is protein-poorer than plasma and mediates material exchange.
options.feedback: Correct: Oxygen, glucose and other substrates move from capillary blood through interstitial fluid to cells, while carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes travel in reverse following gradients and transport processes. Not all exchanges are free passive diffusion, since specialized cell membrane carriers also matter. Cells depend on circulation to renew surrounding fluid.

options.text: Tissue fluid contains the same red-cell concentration as whole blood.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Red blood cells remain inside intact capillaries; most plasma proteins are retained, so tissue fluid is not whole blood leaking into tissue. The proposed answer, “Tissue fluid contains the same red-cell concentration as whole blood.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Tissue fluid and blood plasma contain the same concentration of every plasma protein.
options.feedback: Most large plasma proteins remain within vessels, leaving tissue fluid comparatively protein-poor.

options.text: Oxygen reaches cells without travelling through extracellular fluid.
options.feedback: Oxygen passes from blood through tissue fluid before crossing the cell membrane.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from lymphatic capillaries return excess tissue fluid?

options.text: Valved lymphatics collect interstitial fluid and return it to blood circulation.
options.feedback: Correct: Lymphatic collecting vessels contain valves to restrict backflow, and surrounding muscle movement helps propel lymph through larger ducts that empty into the venous circulation. Failure of drainage can cause tissue swelling. Lymph is not pumped by a four-chambered organ in the same way that blood is.

options.text: Lymph flows outward to soil through xylem vessels.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Lymphatic capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid and proteins; the final return is to large veins, not directly to the left ventricle. The proposed answer, “Lymph flows outward to soil through xylem vessels.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Lymphatic capillaries have thick impermeable walls like large arteries.
options.feedback: Initial lymphatics have thin endothelial walls with entry gaps or overlapping flaps.

options.text: The left ventricle pumps lymph through the lymphatic system.
options.feedback: Skeletal movement, pressure differences and one-way lymphatic valves support lymph return.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from single fish versus double mammalian circulation?

options.text: Fish have a single circulation; mammals have separate pulmonary and systemic circuits.
options.feedback: Correct: In mammals, blood flows through two circuits: right heart → lungs → left heart, then left heart → systemic tissues → right heart. Separation allows high pressure for systemic transport and lower pressure in the pulmonary bed. Draw flow with named organs and distinguish the direction of blood flow from its changing oxygen status.

options.text: Fish have two fully independent ventricular pumps.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Fish blood normally passes gill capillaries before systemic tissues, whereas mammalian blood returns to the heart between pulmonary and systemic capillary beds. The proposed answer, “Fish have two fully independent ventricular pumps.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Bony fish blood returns to the heart between gills and body tissues.
options.feedback: Fish blood passes from the gills directly to systemic tissues before returning to the heart.

options.text: Mammals have only one blood circuit through lung and body in series.
options.feedback: Mammals pump through distinct pulmonary and systemic circuits with an intervening return to the heart.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from cardiac valves and chambers keep flow one-way?

options.text: Valves maintain directional flow, while myocardium generates pressure.
options.feedback: Correct: Atrioventricular valves stop regurgitation from ventricles into atria, and semilunar valves prevent blood in large arteries returning into ventricles. The sinoatrial node initiates coordinated electrical activation. Trace venae cavae → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

options.text: The heart septum directly transfers oxygen into blood.
options.feedback: Incorrect: The pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs; the pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. The proposed answer, “The heart septum directly transfers oxygen into blood.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Pulmonary arteries bring oxygenated blood from lungs to the left atrium.
options.feedback: Pulmonary veins do that; pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to lungs.

options.text: Heart valves are active pumps that generate the blood pressure.
options.feedback: Cardiac myocardium generates pressure; valves respond passively to pressure differences.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from cardiac cycle: filling, pressure and ejection?

options.text: Pressure changes determine valve state through the cardiac cycle.
options.feedback: Correct: During ventricular relaxation, falling pressure closes the aortic valve, and later the mitral valve opens as ventricular pressure drops below atrial pressure. Systolic blood pressure is the higher arterial pressure during ventricular ejection; diastolic pressure is the lower value during relaxation. A reading of 120/80 mmHg is an example, not a required norm.

options.text: AV valves must remain open during ventricular ejection.
options.feedback: Incorrect: The mitral valve opens during ventricular filling only after ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure; it is not opened actively by a muscle. The proposed answer, “AV valves must remain open during ventricular ejection.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: The aortic valve opens before ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
options.feedback: The valve opens only once ventricular pressure is higher than pressure in the aorta.

options.text: Diastolic arterial pressure is the maximum pressure during ventricular ejection.
options.feedback: Systolic pressure is the higher arterial pressure; diastolic pressure is the lower value between beats.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from root pressure operates when transpiration is weak?

options.text: Ion transport can generate positive xylem pressure when evaporation-driven tension is low.
options.feedback: Correct: Water entry can generate positive hydrostatic pressure in xylem, sometimes causing guttation or upward sap movement. Root pressure is most evident when transpirational pull is low, such as on humid nights or early spring before leaves expand. It does not explain water ascent to great heights in actively transpiring tall trees.

options.text: Root pressure is the principal force in every tall tree at midday.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Root pressure is positive hydrostatic pressure from solute accumulation; evaporation-driven cohesion–tension instead operates at negative pressures. The proposed answer, “Root pressure is the principal force in every tall tree at midday.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Root pressure and transpiration pull are both negative pressures.
options.feedback: Root pressure is positive hydrostatic pressure; transpiration pull creates tension.

options.text: Root pressure explains water ascent in the tallest trees during maximum transpiration.
options.feedback: Root pressure is most evident when transpiration is weak and cannot explain ascent to the highest canopies.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from companion cells drive phloem translocation?

options.text: Living sieve elements and metabolically active companion cells support pressure-flow translocation.
options.feedback: Correct: ATP-dependent loading of sucrose at a source raises osmotic concentration, encouraging water entry from xylem and raising turgor pressure. Phloem sap flows by bulk mass flow toward lower-pressure sinks, where solutes are unloaded for use or storage. The direction of a given sieve tube depends on source–sink relations, not simply gravity.

options.text: Sieve tubes are dead lignified xylem vessels.
options.feedback: Incorrect: Sucrose can move toward different sinks in different sieve tubes; a plant does not have one universal upward or downward phloem direction. The proposed answer, “Sieve tubes are dead lignified xylem vessels.”, fails to account for this mechanism.

options.text: Phloem sieve elements are dead lignified tubes identical to xylem.
options.feedback: Mature sieve elements remain alive and depend on companion cells.

options.text: Every sieve tube transports assimilates upward from roots to leaves.
options.feedback: Direction depends on source–sink relations and can differ among sieve tubes.
